content: Ceftriaxone is an antibiotic approved by the FDA for treating various infections, including lower respiratory tract infections, acute bacterial otitis media, skin infections, urinary tract infections, pelvic inflammatory disease, bacterial septicemia, bone and joint infections, intra-abdominal infections, meningitis, and for surgical prophylaxis. It is available for intravenous (IV) or intramuscular (IM) administration. However, the pharmacy bulk package is intended for IV infusion preparation only. Before initiating treatment with ceftriaxone, appropriate specimens should be collected to identify the causative organism and determine its susceptibility to the drug. Therapy may begin before susceptibility test results are available. Ceftriaxone should be administered via IV infusion over 30 minutes. Dilution with calcium-containing solutions, such as Ringer's or Hartmann's solutions, is contraindicated due to the risk of precipitation. Ceftriaxone and calcium-containing solutions must not be administered simultaneously, even via a Y-site. Sequential administration is permissible in non-neonatal patients if the infusion lines are thoroughly flushed with a compatible fluid. Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in patients with known allergies to cephalosporins and in hyperbilirubinemic neonates, especially premature infants, due to the risk of bilirubin displacement and kernicterus. Neonates requiring calcium-containing IV solutions should not receive ceftriaxone due to the risk of ceftriaxone-calcium precipitation, which has been associated with fatal outcomes in some cases. No similar reports exist for non-neonatal patients. Common adverse reactions include erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, pseudomembranous enterocolitis, hemolytic anemia, hypersensitivity reactions, kernicterus, renal failure, and lung injury. Immune-mediated hemolytic anemia has been reported, including severe and fatal cases. If anemia develops during ceftriaxone therapy, the drug should be discontinued until the cause is determined. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including ceftriaxone. CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile may lead to increased morbidity and mortality. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even up to two months after administration. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued, and appropriate management, including fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, and antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, should be initiated. Ceftriaxone therapy should generally continue for at least two days after the resolution of infection symptoms. The usual duration of therapy ranges from 4 to 14 days, with longer durations required for complicated infections. For infections caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, therapy should last at least 10 days. No dosage adjustment is necessary for patients with renal or hepatic impairment. For surgical prophylaxis, a single 1 g dose administered IV 30 minutes to 2 hours before surgery is recommended. The usual adult daily dose is 1 to 2 g once daily or in equally divided doses twice daily, depending on the type and severity of the infection. The total daily dose should not exceed 4 g. For infections caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), a daily dose of 2 to 4 g is recommended to achieve >90% target attainment. Ceftriaxone has no activity against Chlamydia trachomatis. When treating pelvic inflammatory disease or other infections where C. trachomatis is a suspected pathogen, appropriate antichlamydial coverage should be added. In pediatric patients, the recommended total daily dose for skin and skin structure infections is 50 to 75 mg/kg, given once daily or in equally divided doses twice daily, not exceeding 2 g daily. For serious infections other than meningitis, the same dosage range applies, divided every 12 hours. For meningitis, an initial dose of 100 mg/kg (not exceeding 4 g) is recommended, followed by a total daily dose of 100 mg/kg/day (not exceeding 4 g daily), administered once daily or in equally divided doses every 12 hours. Therapy duration is typically 7 to 14 days. Ceftriaxone is physically incompatible with vancomycin, amsacrine, aminoglycosides, and fluconazole in admixtures. When co-administering these drugs, they should be given sequentially with thorough flushing of the IV lines using a compatible fluid. Additionally, ceftriaxone should not be mixed or piggybacked with other antimicrobial drugs or diluents not listed as compatible. Ceftriaxone has been shown to be compatible with Flagyl®-IV (metronidazole hydrochloride) at specific concentrations. However, metronidazole concentrations greater than 8 mg/mL will precipitate, and refrigeration of the admixture should be avoided to prevent precipitation.
